Q1 2025 Foodtech VC Trends
VC activity
VC funding starts slow 
Foodtech VC activity slowed significantly in Q1, with $1.4 billion invested across 202 deals—a 
quarter-over-quarter decline of 49.6% in capital and 15.1% in deal count. Investor caution remains 
elevated, with a marked shift toward more mature startups boasting proven business models. This 
has led to a sharp reduction in seed and early-stage funding. Notably, some investors have pulled 
back from foodtech—or from venture capital altogether. As illustrated in the “Count of unique VC 
investors that invested in foodtech target companies by close year” chart, the number of unique 
VC investors participating in foodtech VC deals dropped 54% from its 2021 peak through Q1 2024, 
while participating nontraditional investors declined 67%.
PitchBook data reveals that 71% of all venture capital deployed in Q1 went to AI & machine learning 
(ML) startups. Foodtech, by contrast, has seen fewer AI-native startups close major rounds. 
As capital increasingly gravitates toward AI, generalist investors may be overlooking attractive 
foodtech opportunities to get AI exposure. However, AI applications in restaurant management 
software, food intelligence & production, and supply chain traceability could reignite interest in 
the sector.
Despite the slowdown, notable deals demonstrate ongoing opportunities. Tapcheck, an earned 
wage access platform for restaurants and retailers, led the quarter with a $250 million Series A 
through a combination of debt ($200 million credit facility) and $50 million in equity. Dorsia, a 
membership platform for exclusive restaurant reservations, raised a $50.4 million Series A at a 
$146 million valuation. Late-stage unicorns Augury and GrubMarket both closed rounds as they 
await exit opportunities. Importantly, these deals came without a valuation cut, bucking 2024’s 
trend of down rounds for maturing startups.

Q1 2025 Foodtech VC Trends
VC ACTIVITY
The current trends in foodtech VC funding have significant implications for both investors and 
startups. For investors, the sharp rise in median valuations signals a flight to quality, with capital 
being concentrated in fewer, more mature startups that can demonstrate proven business models 
and scalability. For example, the overall median pre-money valuation reached $26.3 million in Q1 
2025, which more than doubles that of 2021 during the COVID-19-era. This heightened selectivity 
means investors are likely to face less competition in early-stage deals but may need to pay a 
premium for access to high-potential later-stage companies. As deal sizes also increase, investors 
must conduct deeper due diligence to ensure these higher valuations are justified by strong 
fundamentals and clear paths to profitability.
For startups, the environment is increasingly challenging, especially at the early stage, where 
median valuations have dropped to $6.1 million from $12.1 million in 2021, reflecting tougher 
fundraising conditions and elevated expectations from investors. Startups must demonstrate not 
only innovation but also clear market traction, operational efficiency, and alignment with major 
trends such as sustainability, health, and supply chain resilience to stand out. Those able to meet 
these demands may benefit from larger check sizes and stronger investor support, while those 
unable to show near-term viability may struggle to secure funding or face pressure to accept lower 
valuations or alternative financing options such as venture debt. Overall, the market is rewarding 
quality and resilience, with both investors and startups needing to adapt to a more competitive 
and discerning funding landscape.
Alt-proteins remain resilient
Mature alt-protein companies faced significant challenges at the beginning of the year. Beyond 
Meat reported its third consecutive quarterly revenue decline, contributing to a $1.1 million  loss, 
and subsequently raised $100 million in debt from a sustainable food nonprofit.1 On the private 
market side, mycelium meat alternative producer Meati encountered severe financial challenges 
and lost much of its cash to technical default and selling its assets for just $4 million,2 despite 
having raised over $500 million in VC funding and achieving retail success, selling in over 7,000 
stores across the US.3 
Despite these challenges, early-stage dealmaking in alt-proteins remains robust, particularly in 
fermentation. Liberation Labs and Vivici raised $52 million and $33.8 million early-stage rounds, 
respectively. Liberation Labs plans to operate as a contract manufacturer, producing food 
ingredients and industrial products. Vivici, a customer of Liberation Labs,4 develops fermented 
dairy proteins. Other notable deals included cultivated meat producer Aleph Farm’s $29 million 
Series C and plant-protein producer PROJECT EADEN’s $15.5 million Series A. The deals underscore 
sustained investor interest in both consumer brands and enabling infrastructure. 
1: “Beyond Meat® Reports First Quarter 2025 Financial Results,” Beyond Meat, May 7, 2025.
2: “Breaking: Meati Plans ‘Gut-Wrenching’ Mass Layoffs Amid ‘Bank-Induced Crisis,’” AgFunderNews, Elaine Watson, March 7, 2025.
3: Ibid.
4: “Liberation Labs Lands First Customer for Richmond Plant,” Inside Indiana Business, Eric Dick, May 8, 2025.

Q1 2025 Foodtech VC Trends
VC ACTIVITY
Functional foods stand out
Functional foods emerged as one the strongest near-term opportunities in foodtech amid the 
broader funding downturn. Growing consumer prioritization of wellness through diet and demand 
for health-enhancing everyday food products have fueled rapid growth in this segment.5 PepsiCo’s 
$1.7 billion acquisition of Poppi at a 3.3x revenue multiple underscores the sector’s value and could 
spur further acquisitions as major brands look to expand their functional food portfolios. 
Olipop, a Poppi competitor, raised $137.9 million in a Series C1, achieving unicorn status with an 
estimated $2 billion valuation—a 4.1x revenue multiple. Other notable rounds include Supergut’s 
$22 million Series B and hiyo’s $19 million Series A, both targeting the growing market for 
functional beverages and gut health.
Strategic M&A drives exit activity
Public market volatility kept the IPO window closed across Q1, leaving M&A as the primary exit 
route. We tracked 23 acquisitions of VC-backed foodtech companies in the quarter—not including 
the PepsiCo-Poppi deal, which is still in progress. Wonder made its fifth acquisition, purchasing 
Tastemade, a food-and-travel-focused media company. With past acquisitions including Blue 
Apron and Grubhub, Wonder continues to expand beyond its food hall model—a strategy that 
appears to be working as the company recently raised $600 million at a $7 billion valuation. 
LG Electronics’ acquisition of Bear Robotics and DoorDash’s billion-dollar-plus acquisitions of 
Deliveroo and SevenRooms underscore ongoing consolidation and the expansion of delivery 
incumbents into broader restaurant operations. 
As public markets begin to stabilize, IPO momentum is building across the broader VC ecosystem. 
While no foodtech IPOs are imminent, successful listings in other sectors will serve as important 
market tests. According to PitchBook’s Exit Predictor, Trax Retail, GrubMarket, and Apeel are likely 
IPO candidates. 
5: “Repackaging Diet Culture: How ‘Functional’ Food Took Over the Snack Aisle,” Food & Wine, Audrey Morgan, May 14, 2025.
